source.title: Representing Beauty: Towards a Participatory but Objective Latent Aesthetics

record.tranche_reason: The study measures cross-model representational alignment and reports that alignment varies with aesthetic content, semantic tightness, and layer. It also examines whether input-domain familiarity accounts for the aesthetic result.
record.gate_note: The study reports cross-model alignment results in Figures 1, 2, 4, and 5, and an MMD analysis of input-domain familiarity in Figure 3. The cited convergence findings from other papers are not included as results. No values used only to select settings are recorded.
record.test_reason: The study measures mutual-nearest-neighbour alignment between DINOv2-Large and CLIP, MobileCLIP, ChineseCLIP and VICReg on different input subsets. Alignment changes with the inputs: aesthetic vs unaesthetic or ambiguous AVA images, ImageNet subsets with fewer vs more classes, semantically controlled AVA+APDDv2 sets, and by layer. This bears directly on V6's data-dependence part. No other version is tested by the results.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that aesthetic images produce higher cross-model alignment, persisting under semantic-cluster control and with the Asian-art APDDv2 set. They argue domain familiarity does not explain this, and that semantic tightness of inputs raises measured convergence. From this they argue for an objective but human-mediated basis of beauty, which they cast as hylomorphic rather than Platonic, and for human curation as a driver of convergence.
record.recipe_differences: Uses cross-model mutual-nearest-neighbor alignment, following Huh et al., but tests aesthetic and unaesthetic image groups, uses DINOv2-Large as a reference, and adds layerwise, semantic-tightness, and domain-familiarity analyses. It does not reproduce a model-size or capability sweep.
record.method_sensitivity: Alignment varies with the input group (aesthetic, unaesthetic, or ambiguous), semantic tightness of the input set, and layer. The paper reports one similarity measure and does not compare its settings with alternative similarity measures.

fits_no_version.finding: By MMD against a 4000-class ImageNet subset, aesthetic AVA images are less in-domain than unaesthetic ones, yet they yield higher cross-model alignment.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Higher cross-model alignment on an input subset is not explained by that subset being more in-domain; the more out-of-domain subset can align more.

record.problems: Reported alignment values are not stated in the text and are presented in figures. The text describes some results only in aggregate. The study does not sweep model scale or measure model capability, and it uses a single alignment measure.

untested.parts: Only one similarity measure (mutual kNN) is used. Its settings (k) are not varied. No alternative metrics are compared, and alignment is not measured on deliberately out-of-distribution inputs.
No image-caption paired alignment across model quality; only image encoders are compared.

No measure of how complete alignment is or whether it plateaus. No test of shared training data or objectives as the cause of convergence. The MMD analysis only addresses the aesthetic-vs-unaesthetic gap.

missing.what: Per-model and per-subset alignment values and the model list for Figures 2, 4 and 5. The text gives only aggregate directions, so the size of the input effect cannot be compared across studies.

record.verdict_notes: The paper is a short philosophy-of-art paper. All results are figure-only with no numbers or uncertainty, and the model sizes of the comparison models are not stated. The reader's V6 limits_scope label is replaced: the layer, semantic-tightness and controlled-set results all show input dependence, which is what V6 states. Parts of V6 that were not examined (other metrics, k) are listed as untested, not as limits. The V7 label is dropped: no row measures causes of overall convergence or its completeness. The MMD result, if anything, sits awkwardly with V6's 'weakens out of distribution' clause, but it is not a direct alignment-OOD test.

versions.untested_parts: No sweep over model size or capability, and no result showing whether alignment rises as models become larger or more capable.
No alignment measurement between image representations and paired caption representations as vision and language models improve.
No comparison of different initialization seeds for the same architecture.
No mapping, stitching, relative-representation, or unpaired-translation test.
No analysis of recurring interpretable features, neurons, SAE features, or circuits.
The study varies input groups, semantic tightness, and layer, but does not compare alternative similarity measures or report whether the trend vanishes out of distribution.

It does not establish whether alignment is far from complete or plateaus, and does not test shared objectives as an explanation. Its training-data analysis is limited to input-domain familiarity for the aesthetic-image result.

rows.note: The authors state that unaesthetic images are actually more in-domain than aesthetic images. The paper uses this to argue that greater familiarity with aesthetic images is unlikely to explain the aesthetic alignment result.

relationships.condition: DINOv2-Large vs CLIP, MobileCLIP, ChineseCLIP and VICReg, on AVA aesthetic vs unaesthetic/ambiguous subsets, across layers
relationships.reason: Measured alignment is distinctly higher on aesthetic than other AVA subsets for every comparison model and across layers (figure-only values); r1-r14.
relationships.display_finding: DINOv2-Large alignment was higher on aesthetic AVA images than unaesthetic or ambiguous images across every comparison model and layer.

relationships.condition: Equal-size ImageNet subsets varying in class count; semantically controlled AVA+APDDv2 sets
relationships.reason: Fewer-class subsets give higher convergence (r15), and an aesthetic gap persists after one-image-per-class control (r17). Measured convergence depends on the input set.
relationships.display_finding: Subsets with fewer classes produced higher convergence, and the aesthetic alignment gap persisted after restricting sampling to one image per class.
